Question D2:
D2 — Webhook retries: what delivery guarantee do receivers get?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", `processWebhookJob()` rewrite (PLAN.md:17-18).
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent once; if it fails, it is gone. Once you add retries, a request that timed out after the receiver already processed it will be sent again, so receivers can see the same event twice. You have to choose: keep "never twice" (and accept "sometimes never"), or move to "always at least once" and give receivers a stable key so they can ignore the duplicate. The plan is silent, which means the choice gets made by accident in code.
Stakes if we pick wrong: duplicate webhooks double-charge or double-notify downstream customers; or, in the other direction, transient network blips silently drop events customers were promised.
Recommendation: A because retries exist to survive timeouts, and a stable idempotency key plus a persisted delivered marker is the industry-standard way to make at-least-once safe for receivers.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=7/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) At-least-once + idempotency key + sent-marker (recommended) (human: ~2 days / CC: ~40 min)
  ✅ Transient failures and timeouts are retried, so customers receive events they were promised
  ✅ Stable idempotency header lets receivers dedupe; delivered marker stops our own re-send after a late 2xx
  ❌ Needs a small schema change (delivered marker) and a documented header contract for receivers
B) Strict at-most-once (retry pre-send only) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Preserves today's guarantee exactly; receivers see no behavior change and need no dedupe work
  ✅ Simplest to test: a retry can never follow a sent request
  ❌ Network timeouts and 5xx from the receiver are never retried; those events are lost and only visible in logs or dead-letter
C) At-least-once, no dedupe (human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Least code: just let the retry hook wrap the whole job
  ✅ Events are never silently lost on transient faults
  ❌ Receivers get duplicates with no key to dedupe on; double side-effects downstream are our fault and invisible to us
Net: A costs a marker column and a header contract; B keeps today's promise but keeps today's silent drops; C ships fastest and pushes duplicate bugs onto every receiver.
Header: Webhook semantics
Options:
A) At-least-once + idempotency key + sent-marker
Retry every failure including timeouts. Each delivery carries a stable idempotency header derived from the event/job id (not the attempt). Persist a delivered marker on 2xx before the job returns; the retry path checks the marker and skips the send if set. Document the header for receivers. Human: ~2 days / CC: ~40 min. Risk: low-medium (one schema change).
B) Strict at-most-once (retry pre-send only)
Preserve today's guarantee. Retry only failures that occur before the HTTP request leaves (payload fetch, graph build, serialization). Any failure after send is logged and dead-lettered, never resent. Human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min. Risk: low; transient receiver faults drop events as they do today.
C) At-least-once, no dedupe
Wrap the whole job in the retry hook with no idempotency header and no delivered marker. Receivers may receive duplicates and cannot dedupe them. Human: ~0.5 day / CC: ~10 min. Risk: high for downstream side-effects.

REVIEWED_TREE: 7eb34e9e9d9aaa17ee0bad89281392cd611f15f2 /workspace/gstack-evals

**Scope.** I read the full diff against 97e4796 for every source file: `src/waste/crewlog.ts`, `src/waste/README.md`, `src/cli.ts`, `src/errors/codes.ts` and `docs/errors.md`. The test files were reviewed in summary mode only, so the coverage reduction is visible: `tests/waste/crewlog.test.ts` (+378, 48 tests on shell parsing, bash traits, thread exports, receipts, per-PR data and CLI errors) and `tests/cli.test.ts` (+1/-1, adds `waste` to PLANNED). At this tree, `bun test tests/waste tests/cli.test.ts` passes (48/48), and so do `bun run typecheck` and `bun run errors:check`. I checked findings against real inputs where I could: this crew's thread export shape, 11 gstack-evals PR bodies, the 7 FOUN-64 per-PR data files, and gstack 1.93.39.0's receipt code. I left no changes in the tree.

**1. R5 drops every PR with zero fix-checks from the rounds count, which inflates the past-cap share. FIXABLE.**
crewlog.ts:618-619 and 625-626 (`receiptLoop`) and 730-731 (`scanPrs`) only compute rounds when `fix_checks` is present. gstack leaves it out when it is 0 (`if (fixChecks) out.fix_checks = fixChecks;`, review-scope.ts:458). `REVIEW_LOOP:` lines never print `rounds=` and also leave out a zero `fix_checks`. gstack's own rule is `rounds ?? passes + (fix_checks ?? 0)` (ship-receipt-depth.ts:259).
- **Real receipts:** PR #110's receipt (`passes:1`, no `fix_checks` or `rounds`) comes back with `rounds: null`.
- **FOUN-64 data:** `waste prs` measures rounds for 12 of 31 receipt PRs in gbrain, 13 of 20 in gstack-evals and 20 of 37 in [name removed]. Overall it reports 27 of 45 PRs past the cap (60%, mean 3.71 rounds). gstack's rule over the same data gives 30 of 88 (34%, mean 2.72).

The dropped PRs are the low-round ones, so this is selection bias in the in-the-wild R5 baseline, not random noise. Fix: use gstack's fallback in all three places. If an older receipt's missing field really means "unknown", count it in a visible lower-bound bucket instead of dropping it. Severity: High. Blocks: yes (the next step publishes exactly this number from exactly this data).

**2. R1 cannot see re-runs of test runners that print timings. INVESTIGATE.**
Two back-to-back `bun test tests/waste | tail -4` runs with no change between them differ only in `[32.00ms]` vs `[25.00ms]`. Scanning them gives `r1_checks: 0, informative_reruns: 1`. README:42 labels that bucket "a flake or a real change", which is wrong for timing noise. jest, vitest, pytest, go test and cargo test all print elapsed times, so `r1_checks` sits near zero for anything but quiet tools like tsc. The GEVA-220 plan's R1 already names a sensitivity reading that runs a frozen normalizer (durations, ISO timestamps, PIDs, temp-path suffixes) before comparing; the reader doesn't implement it. The exact-match primary rule follows the plan, so whether the crew baseline needs the normalized reading is a call for whoever owns the plan. Severity: Medium. Blocks: no.

**3. Substitutions hide tree changes from the lenient R1 boundary. FIXABLE.**
`parseShell` (line 102, and the `$(` handling inside double quotes) keeps `$(...)` and backtick bodies as plain words and never parses them. A run of `bun run typecheck`, then `R=$(python3 scripts/fix_imports.py 2>&1); echo "$R"`, then `bun run typecheck` scores `r1: 1, r1_checks: 1`, even though the script edited the tree. Only `r1_strict` catches it. A related case: inside a `$(cat <<'EOF' ...)` commit message, an apostrophe in the here-doc body throws off `closeParen`'s single-quote scan, so the rest of the command (for example `&& git push`) is swallowed and `pushed_head_checks` undercounts. Smaller gaps: `env -u X git push` and `nice -n 10 cmd` take the flag's value as the program name, and `FIX_FLAGS` treats `python -u -m pytest` (unbuffered output) as an update flag. Fix: parse substitution bodies recursively and merge their traits into the segment. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

**4. Some bad exports are accepted or misreported. FIXABLE.**
An empty export file exits 0 and adds a session with 0 items to the totals, so a failed export step is counted silently. An item with `calls: [null]` (line 490), or a non-string `input.text` reaching `.trim()`, exits through E_INTERNAL saying "a defect in src/waste/crewlog.ts, not in your input". The README promises E_WASTE_INPUT for input problems. Fix: refuse an export with zero items, and check the call shape in `readExport`. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

**5. The output prints model ids taken from the input. FIXABLE.**
Line 486 copies each assistant item's `model` string into the output as an object key. That breaks the README's "never prints any other text from what it reads" claim. A model id that happens to be an inherited property name such as `constructor` also turns that count into a string. It is harmless for real Capy exports, but the privacy promise should either say this or the code should map the ids to a fixed set. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

Recommendation: Fix the R5 rounds fallback at crewlog.ts:619/626/731 because it drops 43 of 88 receipt-bearing PRs in the real FOUN-64 data and reports 60% of PRs past the cap where gstack's own rule gives 34%.

When the create call fails, or is cut off by `qmClient`'s 300 s timeout, `adoptNew()` takes ownership of every such container that appeared during that window. `down()` then runs `docker rm -f` on each one, plus `volume rm -f qm-home-*` and `network rm`. A live trial's QM stack uses the same label (`capture.sh:20`), so one failed s1 create during a trial deletes that trial's sandbox and its home volume. The lock does not help, because it only excludes other qm-gstack runs. The interface comment and the new README line ("never another stack's") claim more than the code does. Fix: add `--filter ancestor=<sandboxImage>` to the adoption query. s1's image `harness-eval/qm-sandbox:gstack-<ref8>` is unique to it, and the project lock already rules out a second s1. Alternatively, filter on whatever label QM puts on sandboxes to tie them to their core. FIXABLE. Severity: Medium. Blocks: no, because it needs a concurrent QM stack, which the README already says not to run.

2. **One bad container name skips the whole teardown** (`qm-stack.ts:105`, `108`, `123`). `own()` throws for any name that is not `qm-sbx-*`. `adoptNew()` calls it inside `down()`'s `finally` before `removeSandboxes()`, `dc down` and `unlock()`. One labelled container with an unexpected name aborts all three steps. Because `stopping` is already true, nothing retries, so pg, core and the owned sandboxes stay running. The same throw inside `createSandbox`'s catch leaves `creating` set, so the same failure repeats at teardown. Fix: skip names that don't match in `adoptNew` instead of throwing, or put each teardown step in its own `try`. FIXABLE. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

3. **A sandbox created after the call is cut off leaks** (`qm-stack.ts:108`, `147`). If the client times out while QM is still creating the container, `adoptNew()` takes its snapshot and sets `creating = null` before the container exists. Nothing tracks it afterwards, and `compose down --remove-orphans` doesn't remove it either, because core created it through the Docker socket and not through compose. Fix: keep the pre-create baseline until `down()`, and diff against it after `dc down` has stopped core. FIXABLE. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

4. **The host lock is not atomic** (`qm-stack.ts:66-76`). The lock code reads the file, checks the pid and then writes, with no `O_EXCL`. Two runs launched close together can both take the lock. The second run's opening `dc down -v --remove-orphans` then removes the first run's stack, which is the exact case the lock exists to stop. `release()` also deletes the file without checking it still holds its own pid, so the run that lost the race clears the winner's lock. Two smaller gaps:
   - The lock directory comes from `tmpdir()`, so a run with `TMPDIR` set and one without lock in different places.
   - A reused pid makes a dead lock look alive.

   Fix: create the file with `writeFileSync(path, pid, { flag: 'wx' })`. On `EEXIST`, check whether the holder is alive, then unlink and retry `wx` once. Release only if the file still holds this process's pid. Use a fixed directory. FIXABLE. Severity: Low. Blocks: no, since this is a manual tool.

Fix: decide the destination for the router the same way as for the receipt, or write it after `ok` is known. FIXABLE. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

6. **`receiptOut` treats an unreadable receipt as permission to overwrite it** (`qm-stack.ts:156-160`). A committed receipt that is missing, has bad JSON, or lacks `gstack.ref` gives `committedRef === null`. Any default run at any ref then overwrites the committed path. Today both committed receipts carry the full sha `21277291c850...` under `gstack.ref`, which matches the newly normalised `ref`, so this is latent. INVESTIGATE: decide whether a parse failure should go to `work` instead. Severity: Low. Blocks: no.

**Scope.** The range fc880c3..HEAD changes two files. `src/trial/review/run.ts` (source) adds each ceo session's `trial.json` and `host/skill-gates/` to the receipts list that `copyToSink` copies, and updates the header comment to match. `tests/trial/review/ceo-followup.test.ts` adds one test, "the receipts sink holds what ceo rows and the gate report read". I reviewed the test and fixture files in summary mode only (diff stat and test names), so their bodies were not part of the adversarial pass.

**Checks.** That test file passes (45 pass, 0 fail) and `bun run typecheck` is clean.

**What holds up.**
- Missing files are fine. `copyToSink` keeps only files that exist, so non-enforced arms with no `skill-gates/`, and sessions with no `trial.json`, copy cleanly.
- Links are fine. `gateRecord`'s `copyTree` copies only regular files and directories, so `host/skill-gates/` can't bring a symlink into the sink. The hard-link check still covers every new target.
- The paths match what the rows read. `trial.json` is written at `spec.dir`, which equals `sessionDir(...)`. That is exactly where `ceo-cli.ts` `gateReport` and `ceoDisk` look.
- No new secret path. `trial.json` holds the record, the delta (path lists only), logs (stderr tails, copy failures) and the gate report. None of these carry the proxy token. Sealed suites are still refused a sink inside the repo.

**Finding 1 (FIXABLE): a re-run session's sink copy mixes the new trial.json with the earlier attempt's files.** `copyToSink` uses `cpSync(..., { recursive: true, force: true })`. That merges into an existing sink directory and never removes what is already there. It also skips sources that are missing this time, so a file the new attempt didn't write keeps the earlier attempt's copy.

I reproduced it with the real `copyToSink`:
1. Attempt 1 wrote `trial.json`, `host/ceo-review/a/ceo-review.md`, `host/skill-gates/OLD/` and `host/transcript.ndjson`, and the run copied them to the sink.
2. Attempt 2 ran in the same session dir (`rmSync(dir)` at run.ts:494) and wrote only a new `trial.json`.
3. After the second copy, the sink held the new `trial.json` plus attempt 1's review copy, gate record and transcript.

Before this diff the sink had no `trial.json`, so `ceoDisk` and `gateReport` reading the sink copy got `copy_failed: true`, and `findings_written` and `gate_armed` read false. Now a fresh `trial.json` with empty `copy_out` vouches for stale `host/ceo-review/` copies and a stale transcript. So `ceo rows` run against the sink can score an attempt-2 journal entry with attempt-1 findings and exposure, and it gives no error.

It's reachable when a run completes, its copy lands, and a later run with the same out dir and sink re-runs sessions (`--repair` on stale cells, or a resume that re-runs non-reused cells). Rows read from the out dir are unaffected.

The fix: in `copyToSink`, or in run.ts before the copy, `rmSync` each session-scoped sink target for every session that ran in this invocation, whether or not its source exists now. Then copy. Add a test that re-runs one session and checks the sink holds no stale `ceo-review/` copy.

Severity: Medium
Blocks: no

**Finding 2 (INVESTIGATE): the sink copy runs only once, at the end of `runReviewUnits` (run.ts:677).** This predates the diff, but the diff raises its stakes. A run that throws mid-way, or a machine that dies mid-way, copies nothing: not the new `trial.json` and gate records, and not even sessions that finished. On an ephemeral VM, every finished session's gate evidence is lost. Copying per session after `runTrial` would close it, but that changes the copy contract, so it needs a call from you.

Severity: Low
Blocks: no

Recommendation: Fix the merge-not-replace sink copy at durable.ts copyToSink (exposed by run.ts:370-373 now copying trial.json) because a re-run session's fresh trial.json makes sink-based ceo rows trust the previous attempt's ceo-review copies and transcript, which silently corrupts findings_written and exposure.

ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if the send fails, it is dropped, never duplicated. Adding retries flips that. Receivers that charge a card or create a record on each webhook will do it twice.
Stakes if we pick wrong: duplicate side effects at every customer receiving your webhooks, with no way for them to tell a retry from a new event.

Pros / cons:
A) Idempotent delivery with per-job delivery record (recommended)
  ✅ Retries recover from transient receiver outages without ever recording two successful deliveries for one job
  ✅ The `Idempotency-Key` header is the standard way webhook receivers dedupe, so well-built receivers drop the duplicate automatically
  ❌ Needs a persisted delivery-state record (pending / delivered / ambiguous) written before each send, plus a migration (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
B) Exclude processWebhookJob from the retry framework
  ✅ Preserves today's at-most-once behavior exactly, so the existing contract and its regression test stay simple
  ✅ Smallest change: this worker just does not wire the retry hook
  ❌ Webhooks still vanish on any transient failure, which is the pain this plan exists to fix
C) At-least-once with no dedup
  ✅ Simplest retry wiring; no delivery table and no header
  ✅ Every job eventually delivers or dead-letters
  ❌ Every ambiguous send produces a visible duplicate at the receiver and pushes the dedup burden onto every customer
Net: one header and one state record versus either keeping the drops or shipping duplicates to customers.
